t: Maximum Number of Operations With the Same Score I
o: Each operation deletes the first two elements and their sum is the operation's score; every operation must share one common score. Crucially, the first operation's score is forced: it is nums[0] + nums[1]. So the question reduces to: how many leading disjoint pairs (nums[0],nums[1]), (nums[2],nums[3]), … have sum equal to that first sum, stopping at the first mismatch? In Example 1 the score is 5 and pairs (3,2),(1,4) both sum to 5, giving 2. In Example 2, (1,5) and (3,3) give 6 but (4,1) breaks the streak, so the answer is 2. With n ≤ 100, any polynomial simulation works.
k: The required score is fixed by the very first pair — there is no choice to optimize.
Operations consume elements strictly from the front in pairs, so a single left-to-right sweep suffices.

a.i: Since the score must equal nums[0] + nums[1], the best strategy is simply to keep deleting front pairs as long as they match that score; deviating is impossible because deletion order is forced. Count consecutive matching pairs.
s: Set target = nums[0] + nums[1], count = 1, i = 2.
While i + 1 < n and nums[i] + nums[i+1] == target, increment count and i by 2.
a.t: O(n) — one pass over the array in steps of two.

a.n: Approach 2: Brute force over candidate scores
a.i: A more general (and instructive) template: try every possible score that could be forced — namely each adjacent-pair sum — and simulate how many consecutive front pairs match it. The answer is the maximum over candidates. This is slower but shows how to handle variants where the first move is optional or the score can be chosen.
s: Collect all adjacent pair sums as candidate scores.
For each candidate s, walk pairs from the front counting how many consecutive pairs sum to s (at least one pair must match for the run to start).
a.t: O(n²) — up to n candidate scores, each simulated in O(n).

w: Always use Approach 1 — the first pair pins the score, making the greedy provably optimal. Common pitfall: forgetting that operations stop when fewer than two elements remain (handled naturally by the loop bound), or mistakenly trying to reorder elements (not allowed). Follow-up: Maximum Number of Operations With the Same Score II, where you may delete any two elements, requiring a DP over chosen scores.
